summary: Contains the requirements that a AAA service must support to help provide Mobile IP services. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When a mobile node uses a network outside its home domain, that network needs to verify the node, decide what it may use and record its service. RFC 2977 describes requirements for the AAA systems that coordinate those tasks.

subtitle: Requirements for authentication, authorization and accounting when Mobile IP users visit another network.

tldr.problem: A mobile node visiting a foreign network needs access decisions and accounting, even though its credentials and home service are managed elsewhere.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes local and home AAA authorities, security relationships, reliable inter-domain messages, Mobile IP registration key distribution and brokers for scaling trust.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2977 lists requirements for AAA services that support Mobile IP. It is a requirements memo, not an AAA protocol specification.

facts.label: Registration security associations
facts.value: Mobile node–home agent, mobile node–foreign agent, and home agent–foreign agent

today: RFC 2977 is an Informational memo published in October 2000. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the document states requirements for AAA support of Mobile IP.

sections.title: The AAA Model for a Visiting Node
sections.content:
Authentication verifies a claimed identity, authorization decides whether a requested right is granted, and accounting records resource use. In the memo's model, a mobile node requests service from an attendant in a foreign domain. A local AAA authority (AAAL) consults the node's home AAA authority (AAAH) when it needs information about the node's credentials.

The attendant needs a security relationship with the AAAL, and the mobile node has a security relationship with its home authority. The AAAL and AAAH also need a secure relationship to exchange authentication and authorization information. The memo says requiring every pair of authorities to establish a direct relationship does not scale.
sections.plainLanguage: A visited network can ask a local AAA authority to check a mobile node with its home AAA authority. The attendant, local authority and home authority need secure ways to exchange the decision.

sections.title: Requirements for AAA Messages
sections.content:
An AAA protocol must provide reliable transport with hop-by-hop retransmission and failover, and deliver responses soon enough to avoid Mobile IP timeouts. It should allow acknowledgements to be carried in AAA messages and support certificates to reduce the number of message exchanges.

The protocol must provide hop-by-hop message integrity and identity authentication. It must support replay protection, matching accounting messages to earlier authorization messages, and real-time accounting with timestamps. Accounting can use bilateral arrangements or broker AAA servers for clearing and reconciliation.
sections.plainLanguage: AAA messages must be delivered reliably, checked for tampering and replay, and tied to the correct user. Accounting records need timestamps and a way to match them to authorization.

sections.title: IP Addresses and Mobile Identity
sections.content:
AAA servers must be able to obtain or coordinate an IP address for a client when requested. They must also identify a client by something other than its IP address. The memo describes the Network Access Identifier (NAI), commonly written as user@realm, which lets the local authority identify the client's home domain.

The home AAA authority may coordinate an address with a home agent. The memo also describes cases where the local authority provides a local home agent or where local payment allows the local authority to handle authorization without contacting the home authority.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node can identify itself with a name such as user@realm, rather than relying on its current IP address. AAA servers can coordinate address allocation and, in some cases, a home agent.

sections.title: Mobile IP Registration and Key Setup
sections.content:
During initial registration, AAA servers enable authentication, authorize the mobile node's use of resources, and initiate accounting. AAA and Mobile IP work should be processed during one Internet traversal when possible, but AAA servers must not process Mobile IP messages intended for mobility agents. Mobile IP data carried through AAA servers is opaque to them.

For later registrations, the initial exchange must establish or identify security associations for the mobile node with its home agent, the mobile node with its foreign agent, and the home agent with the foreign agent. The memo notes that later registrations can proceed without further AAA involvement once the necessary state is established.
sections.plainLanguage: Initial registration sets up the security relationships needed for later Mobile IP registrations. AAA servers authorize the request and coordinate keying information, but do not interpret Mobile IP data passed through them.

sections.title: Brokers for Many Domains
sections.content:
Direct trust relationships between local and home AAA authorities can grow quadratically as the number of domains increases. A broker AAA server (AAAB) can provide a shared contact point, allowing domains to cooperate without each having a direct relationship with every other domain. The memo says multiple broker layers must be supported in diverse provider networks.

A broker may relay messages between domains or help them establish an end-to-end security association. It must be able to pass encrypted data such as registration keys. The memo notes that brokers can add messages and latency, especially during initial access.
sections.plainLanguage: A broker can let many domains coordinate without each building a direct trust relationship with every other domain. Brokers must pass protected data, and their involvement can add messages and delay.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
The document sets requirements for a security-driven AAA service; it does not define the mechanisms that satisfy them. Adding authorities and brokers also requires administration of security relationships among those entities.

For IPv6 Mobile IP, the memo notes there is no foreign agent. It says the attendant role must instead be provided elsewhere, such as by a local router or DHCPv6 server.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo describes requirements rather than specifying an AAA protocol. Its IPv6 discussion notes that the attendant role must be provided without a foreign agent.
